name: Ahmed al-Sharaa
role: President of Syria (2025–); former leader of Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham (as Abu Mohammad al-Jolani)
summary: Al-Sharaa moved from leading an al-Qaeda-linked jihadist group to governing Syria as a Sunni Islamist-rooted but pragmatic president. His record shows a centralised presidential system with Islamic jurisprudence as the main source of law, a state monopoly on arms, a turn to free markets and foreign investment, and a security-first, non-confrontational line toward Israel.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: At the 2026 Arab Media Summit he described Syria moving from a socialist economic model to a free-market system with a larger private-sector role.

central-planning.rationale: In the same 2026 speech he described leaving the socialist (state-run) model for a free-market system, which rejects central planning.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: He has courted Gulf and European investors, citing the DP World link to Tartous port; he did not speak about limits on buying strategic firms, so this is only a low-confidence reading of an open-door stance.

refugee-return.rationale: In his interview with The New Arab he said refugees have a right to return voluntarily and with dignity and that most Syrians would come back if conditions allowed. He did not mention descendants.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: From December 2024 he folded rebel factions into the Defense Ministry, and the constitutional declaration he issued (Article 9) bars individuals and groups from forming armed forces.

revolution-justified.rationale: He led the armed offensive that overthrew Assad and in September 2025 said his government 'emerged from a revolution' and must reflect the people's voice.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: The constitutional declaration he issued makes Islamic jurisprudence the main source of legislation; asked about applying Islamic law he deferred to experts, and the declaration also keeps rights guarantees, so it falls short of full scriptural law.

separate-church-state.rationale: The declaration he issued requires the president to be Muslim and sets Islamic jurisprudence as the main source of law, and a Fatwa Council reviews laws, so religion and state are not strictly separated.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: The declaration he issued lets religious communities keep their own personal status laws instead of one civil law for all.

women-suffrage.rationale: The declaration he issued commits the state to women's political rights, and the 2025 election decree set a target for women among electors; women stood in the October 2025 vote.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The declaration he issued gives citizens equal rights and duties regardless of race, religion, gender or lineage, but it also requires a Muslim president and restricts rights on security and morals grounds.

separated-powers.rationale: The declaration provides for separation of powers and judicial independence, but the president appoints ministers, the constitutional court and a third of the Assembly, so the record is contested.

consent-of-governed.rationale: In September 2025 he said his government must reflect the voice of the people; he did not otherwise state a theory of legitimacy.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: At the UN in September 2025 he promised to bring to justice anyone with Syrians' blood on their hands and gave the UN a right to investigate; the declaration he issued created a Transitional Justice Commission. He did not specifically address international courts.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: In September 2025 he said he might discuss the Golan if Israel de-escalates, and in July 2026 that a security deal would not give up Syria's right to the Golan; the statements point both ways.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Al Jazeera reported that he called the Golan Heights occupied and said a deal would not compromise Syria's right to them; the report is a paraphrase, and he did not discuss consent of the population.

return-lost-territory.rationale: He has said Syria's claim to the Golan Heights remains, but has not demanded its return and is pursuing a security agreement without confrontation.

right-to-secede.rationale: The declaration he issued calls Syria indivisible and criminalizes calls for secession; in November 2025 he said the coast cannot be run by an independent authority isolated from other regions.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: His government pressed the Kurdish-led SDF militarily in early 2026 before an integration agreement, and he rejected an isolated coastal authority; he did not frame force as a response to secession specifically.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: He called for a strong centralised state and said the coast cannot be run by an independent authority; the Kurdish autonomy rejection is reported in paraphrase. His January 2026 decree gives cultural, not territorial, rights.

decide-locally.rationale: He has backed a strong centralised state and said the coast cannot be governed separately from other regions.

minority-language-support.rationale: In January 2026 he issued a decree making Kurdish a national language alongside Arabic that schools may teach, and banning ethnic or linguistic discrimination.

single-official-language.rationale: His January 2026 decree names Kurdish a national language alongside Arabic and permits teaching in it, rather than making one language the sole common medium.

ban-cartels.rationale: The declaration he issued says the economy rests on fair competition and bans monopolies.

party-controls-media.rationale: The declaration he issued guarantees press and information freedom, and he said media should avoid politicization; no ruling party exists to control it.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Under the declaration he issued, the president is supreme commander of the armed forces and declares mobilization with National Security Council approval.

notes: Positions changed sharply: answers use his most recent statements as president (2025-2026). His earlier jihadist statements were not the latest record on any answered topic. Many topics (social issues, taxes, welfare, most foreign policy) are null because he has made no direct statement; several later-reported items (Chatham House 2026) were reachable only through secondary summaries and were not used.
